messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 31
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Carpenter
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 42

James is thirty-one years old, a carpenter, and he has been married to his wife, Linh, for six years. He came to see me after his primary care doctor suggested it, following months of insomnia and a persistent, gnawing tightness in his chest that no physical exam could explain. He is a quiet man, with calloused hands that he keeps folded in his lap, and he speaks in a low, measured voice.

The event that broke something in him happened a little over a year ago. He had been working late on a custom bookshelf for a client in a neighborhood he didn’t usually work in. It was a warm night, and he was loading his tools into the back of his truck when he saw two police officers approach a young man on the street corner. James didn’t think much of it at first. He kept working, feeling the familiar weight of his tool belt, the smell of sawdust still clinging to his shirt. Then he heard shouting, a scuffle, and the sharp, terrible sound of something hard hitting flesh. He looked up just as one of the officers drove a baton into the young man’s ribs. The young man crumpled, and James felt a cold jolt of electricity shoot down his own spine.

He didn’t intervene. He didn’t run. He just stood frozen, his hand gripping the handle of his circular saw, watching until the young man was handcuffed and shoved into the back of a cruiser. The officers glanced his way, and James felt his stomach drop. One of them, a large man with a red face, just stared at him for a long moment. James looked away first. He got in his truck and drove home, his hands shaking on the steering wheel.

That was the night the nightmares started. He doesn’t dream of the baton or the shouting. He dreams of the officer’s eyes, the way they looked through him, and the sensation of his own body turning to concrete. He wakes up drenched in sweat, his heart hammering, convinced he can still feel the cold weight of the saw in his hand. He has not touched that particular saw since. It sits on a shelf in his workshop, covered in dust, a monument he cannot bring himself to look at.

At work, he is a different man. He used to love the precision of his craft—the smell of cedar, the satisfying click of a dovetail joint. Now, he finds himself constantly looking over his shoulder. He refuses to take jobs in certain parts of the city, making weak excuses to his boss. The sound of a police siren, even blocks away, makes his throat close up. Last month, a squad car drove slowly past his job site while he was framing a house. He dropped his hammer and climbed down from the scaffolding, telling his foreman he felt sick. He drove home and sat in his truck in the driveway for an hour, unable to go inside.

His relationship with Linh has become strained. She tries to comfort him, but he cannot explain the shame that sits in his gut like a stone. He feels weak for not helping that young man, and he feels terrified that the officers will somehow come for him. He is hypervigilant in a way that exhausts him. He checks the locks on the doors three times before bed. He avoids eye contact with strangers, especially men in uniform. When Linh touches him unexpectedly, he flinches.

He told me, in a voice barely above a whisper, that the worst part is the certainty that it could happen again. That it will happen again. He lives in a state of constant waiting, his body braced for a blow that has already fallen. He is not angry. He is not sad. He is simply afraid, a carpenter who can no longer build anything, trapped in the wreckage of a single, frozen moment.
